Q: Is fetching std::chrono::steady_clock inside a critical section necessary to theoretically align C++ happens-before with real-time order? A:

The inverted execution is legal but your test can't ever print it nothing in the standard says t_clear runs promptly a conforming implementation can just stall it for an hour so #2 happening before #1 needs no time travel, just a slow thread but trace your guard: time_buy = now() → buy_stock → unlock → clear_stock's lock → join → t_clear_complete = now(). That whole chain is happens-before, and [time.clock.req] says happens-before implies t1 <= t2. So in the inverted execution time_buy <= t_clear_complete, duration <= 0, and your if (duration >= 1h) never fires. The only executions that print anything are the ones where #1 happens-before #2 — and then the mutex forces "empty".

Clocks don't create happens-before; happens-before constrains clocks. So the "time-inverted" execution isn't forbidden, it's just unobservable from inside the program any measurement ordered with the events is required to agree with the logical order. clear/ok can't happen.

Q: Can C++ "happens-before" order contradict physical wall-clock execution time? A:

Yes, absolutely. The C++ happens-before relation is a logical synchronization order defined by the memory model—it does not always match physical wall-clock execution time.

Q: MS Access re-uses already established ODBC connections, disregarding differing connection parameters A:

This is expected behaviour. Access caches the connection after the first successful connection to the same database.

Apart from that, it doesn't make much sense to attempt to open several connections to the same database.

More on this: Access Caching ODBC connection settings.

Q: question at / pivot and >> 2 in C++ Solution for Next Higher Number A:

This solution is a combination of purely arithmetic operations (binary addition with carry) and purely bitwise manipulations.

int pivot = n & -n;

Here we get the rightmost set bit. The operation is valid only for representing negative numbers with 2's complement. I'll try to explain this:

-n = ~n + 1

If n has 1 or more zero rightmost bits, then after inversion (~) they will be set to 1. Then, after addition (+ 1), they will become zero again, and the next zero bit will be set. (There is also another explanation here.)

Why do we need this pivot number? The fact is that if we add any number from 1 to pivot - 1 to n, the number of set bits will only increase, because this addition operation will affect only the rightmost zero bits, and will not affect the remaining bits. That is, n + pivot is the minimum possible value.

Next, it will be easier to explain using a specific example: Next, it will be easier to explain using a specific example: Let n = 0b10111000. Let's highlight 3 ranges in the binary representation of this number:

CC BBB AAA
10 111 000

Where A is the rightmost zero bits. B - the nonzero bits following them, C - the remaining bits. Of course, 1 or 2 of these ranges may be empty.

            CC BBB AAA

n         = 10 111 000
pivot     = 00 001 000
n + pivot = 11 000 000

After adding n + pivot, the bits of range B are reset to zero, and the rightmost one bit of range C is set. Range B contains the quantity of bits that must be added to the sum n + pivot minus 1 bit (carried over to the range C) to get the desired number.

n ^ (n + pivot)

The xor (^) operation highlights the changes and resets the untouched bits. That is, it highlights range B and the rightmost 1 bit of range C:

                  CC BBB AAA

n               = 10 111 000
n + pivot       = 11 000 000
n ^ (n + pivot) = 01 111 000

In other words, the number n ^ (n + pivot) contains as many set bits as there are in the range B (see above) plus 1 bit carried over to the range C. It turns out that this number contains 2 more bits than we need.

To get the next number containing the same quantity of bits as n, we need to find the minimum number containing the required quantity of set bits and place it in the range A of the sum (n + pivot). To do this, we need to get rid of the rightmost zero bits in the number n ^ (n + pivot):

                            CC BBB AAA

pivot                     = 00 001 000
(n ^ (n + pivot))         = 01 111 000
(n ^ (n + pivot)) / pivot = 00 001 111

Division / pivot can be represented as / (2^m) or >> m, where m is the quantity of right shifts (equal to the quantity of rightmost zero bits).

Now we need to get rid of the 2 bits that were mentioned above. To do this, we make 2 more right shifts:

 (n ^ (n + pivot)) / pivot       = 00 001 111
((n ^ (n + pivot)) / pivot) >> 2 = 00 000 011   (= before)

All that's left is to combine the result using + or |:

                       CC BBB AAA

n + pivot            = 11 000 000
brfore               = 00 000 011
(n + pivot) | before = 11 000 011
